results.name: exception_first_vs_later_digit
results.description: In 3-4 example sets where all but one example share a last digit d, yes-rate for non-example targets ending in d when the odd example is shown FIRST minus when it is shown later; observed differing from null_mean means the model's order dependence (sticky first guess) is too strong/weak — above means people are less hurt by an early exception than the model predicts.
results.code:
# name: exception_first_vs_later_digit
# description: In 3-4 example sets where all but one example share a last digit d, yes-rate for non-example targets ending in d when the odd example is shown FIRST minus when it is shown later; observed differing from null_mean means the model's order dependence (sticky first guess) is too strong/weak — above means people are less hurt by an early exception than the model predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    isex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    dmin = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    ld = np.mod(E, 10)
    best = np.zeros(len(t)); dig = np.full(len(t), -1.0)
    for k in range(10):
        c = np.sum(ld == k, axis=1)
        upd = c > best
        dig = np.where(upd, k, dig); best = np.where(upd, c, best)
    base = (n >= 3) & (best == n - 1) & ~isex & (np.mod(t, 10) == dig)
    first_odd = ld[:, 0] != dig
    a = base & first_odd; b = base & ~first_odd
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: exception_set_majority_digit_far
results.description: Sets of 3-4 examples in which all but exactly one example share a last digit d: yes-rate for non-example targets ending in d that are >=10 from every example; observed above null_mean means people keep the digit rule despite one exception more than the model (trust/stickiness too low), below means the model over-tolerates the exception.

    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    isex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    dmin = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    ld = np.mod(E, 10)
    best = np.zeros(len(t)); dig = np.full(len(t), -1.0)

        dig = np.where(upd, k, dig); best = np.where(upd, c, best)

results.name: small_rule_set_nonmember_yes
results.description: Sets of >=2 examples all belonging to a small arithmetic rule (squares, cubes, powers of 2/3, or powers of 2 plus 37): yes-rate for non-example targets outside every such rule the set fits; observed below null_mean means people reject off-rule numbers more sharply than the model (model's interval/lapse mass too high for rule-like sets), above means the opposite.
results.code:
# name: small_rule_set_nonmember_yes
# description: Sets of >=2 examples all belonging to a small arithmetic rule (squares, cubes, powers of 2/3, or powers of 2 plus 37): yes-rate for non-example targets outside every such rule the set fits; observed below null_mean means people reject off-rule numbers more sharply than the model (model's interval/lapse mass too high for rule-like sets), above means the opposite.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    isex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    dmin = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    ld = np.mod(E, 10)
    rules = [[k * k for k in range(1, 11)], [1, 8, 27, 64], [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64], [3, 9, 27, 81], [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 37, 64]]
    fits_any = np.zeros(len(t), dtype=bool); t_in = np.zeros(len(t), dtype=bool)
    valid = ~np.isnan(E)
    for R in rules:
        R = np.array(R, float)
        fit = np.all(np.isin(E, R) | ~valid, axis=1)
        fits_any |= fit
        t_in |= fit & np.isin(t, R)
    m = (n >= 2) & fits_any & ~t_in & ~isex
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

results.name: inside_range_gap_vs_near
results.description: Multi-example sets with span >=30: yes-rate for inside-range non-example targets >=10 from the nearest example minus those <=3 from it (targets sharing a last digit with any example excluded); observed below null_mean means people generalise by similarity to individual examples more than the model's flat interval fill, above means people fill gaps more evenly than the model.
results.code:
# name: inside_range_gap_vs_near
# description: Multi-example sets with span >=30: yes-rate for inside-range non-example targets >=10 from the nearest example minus those <=3 from it (targets sharing a last digit with any example excluded); observed below null_mean means people generalise by similarity to individual examples more than the model's flat interval fill, above means people fill gaps more evenly than the model.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    isex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    dmin = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    ld = np.mod(E, 10)
    shares = np.any(ld == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None], axis=1)
    base = (n >= 2) & (hi - lo >= 30) & (t > lo) & (t < hi) & ~isex & ~shares
    a = base & (dmin >= 10); b = base & (dmin <= 3)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: single_example_arithmetic_far
results.description: Single-example sets: yes-rate for targets >10 away, not sharing the example's last digit, that share a small arithmetic rule with it (common multiple-of-m for m in 3..12, square, cube, or power of 2-10); observed above null_mean means the model under-produces arithmetic-rule generalisation from one example, below means it over-produces it.
results.code:
# name: single_example_arithmetic_far
# description: Single-example sets: yes-rate for targets >10 away, not sharing the example's last digit, that share a small arithmetic rule with it (common multiple-of-m for m in 3..12, square, cube, or power of 2-10); observed above null_mean means the model under-produces arithmetic-rule generalisation from one example, below means it over-produces it.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    isex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    dmin = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    ld = np.mod(E, 10)
    x = E[:, 0]
    hit = np.zeros(len(t), dtype=bool)
    for m_ in range(3, 13):
        if m_ == 10:
            continue
        hit |= (np.mod(x, m_) == 0) & (np.mod(t, m_) == 0)
    sq = np.array([k * k for k in range(1, 11)], float)
    cu = np.array([1, 8, 27, 64], float)
    hit |= np.isin(x, sq) & np.isin(t, sq)
    hit |= np.isin(x, cu) & np.isin(t, cu)
    for b in range(2, 11):
        p = np.array([b ** k for k in range(1, 8) if b ** k <= 100], float)
        hit |= np.isin(x, p) & np.isin(t, p)
    m = (n == 1) & hit & (np.abs(t - x) > 10) & (np.mod(t, 10) != np.mod(x, 10))
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

results.name: set_level_yes_rate_sd
results.description: Standard deviation, across example sets with >=20 non-example trials, of the set's yes-rate on non-example targets; observed above null_mean means human generalisation differs between sets more than the model predicts (model too uniform across sets), below means the model exaggerates set-to-set differences.
results.code:
# name: set_level_yes_rate_sd
# description: Standard deviation, across example sets with >=20 non-example trials, of the set's yes-rate on non-example targets; observed above null_mean means human generalisation differs between sets more than the model predicts (model too uniform across sets), below means the model exaggerates set-to-set differences.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    isex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    dmin = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    ld = np.mod(E, 10)
    d = pd.DataFrame({"s": df["number_set"].astype(str).to_numpy(), "r": r})[~isex]
    g = d.groupby("s")["r"].agg(["mean", "count"])
    g = g[g["count"] >= 20]
    if len(g) < 2:
        return 0.0
    return float(g["mean"].std())

results.name: decade_of_shared_last_digit
results.description: Sets of >=2 examples that all end in the same digit d: yes-rate for non-example targets whose tens digit is d but which do not end in d; observed below null_mean means the model over-generalises via "contains digit d" (people read the shared digit as a last-digit rule only), above means it under-generalises.
results.code:
# name: decade_of_shared_last_digit
# description: Sets of >=2 examples that all end in the same digit d: yes-rate for non-example targets whose tens digit is d but which do not end in d; observed below null_mean means the model over-generalises via "contains digit d" (people read the shared digit as a last-digit rule only), above means it under-generalises.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    isex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    dmin = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    ld = np.mod(E, 10)
    same = (n >= 2) & (np.nanmax(ld, axis=1) == np.nanmin(ld, axis=1))
    d = np.nanmin(ld, axis=1)
    m = same & ~isex & (np.floor(t / 10) == d) & (np.mod(t, 10) != d)
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

results.name: boundary_outside_minus_inside
results.description: Multi-example sets: yes-rate for non-example targets 1-5 outside the examples' [min,max] minus yes-rate for targets 1-5 inside the range from the nearest boundary; observed above null_mean means people's range boundary is softer (more extension past the extremes) than the model predicts, below means it is sharper.
results.code:
# name: boundary_outside_minus_inside
# description: Multi-example sets: yes-rate for non-example targets 1-5 outside the examples' [min,max] minus yes-rate for targets 1-5 inside the range from the nearest boundary; observed above null_mean means people's range boundary is softer (more extension past the extremes) than the model predicts, below means it is sharper.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    isex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    dmin = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    ld = np.mod(E, 10)
    dist_b = np.minimum(np.abs(t - lo), np.abs(t - hi))
    inside = (t > lo) & (t < hi)
    outside = (t < lo) | (t > hi)
    base = (n >= 2) & ~isex & (dist_b >= 1) & (dist_b <= 5) & (hi - lo >= 12)
    a = base & outside; b = base & inside
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
